Age-period-cohort model by the intrinsic estimator

Source: R/apcie.R
apcie.Rd

Asks how much of the change in a rate (arrests, imprisonment, victimisation per head) over the years belongs to age, to the period and to the generation (cohort) people were born into. From a table of counts by age group (rows) and period (columns), with equal widths, and the population at risk in each cell, the Poisson log-linear model $$\log E(y_{ij}) = \log(expo_{ij}) + \mu + \alpha_i + \beta_j + \gamma_{j - i + A}$$ has effects of age, period and cohort, each summing to 0. Because cohort = period - age, the three linear trends cannot be told apart: the design has one null direction, and the data fit equally well along it. The intrinsic estimator (Yang, Fu and Land 2004) picks the solution with no component along that direction, the one a principal-components (minimum-norm) fit gives; its covariance is the model-based one projected the same way. The model is fitted by the iteratively reweighted least squares of glm() (as cntreg() fits).

Usage

apcie(y, expo, level = 0.95, maxit = 100)

Arguments

y

The counts: a numeric matrix with one row per age group (youngest first) and one column per period (earliest first), at least three of each, numbers from 0, not all 0. Row and column names label the effects.

expo

The population at risk of each cell: a matrix of the same dimensions, positive.

level

The confidence level of the Wald intervals: one number strictly between 0 and 1.

maxit

The steps of the fit: one whole number from 1.

Value

An object of class apcie, a list: coef, one row for the intercept and for every age group, period and cohort (term, level, est, se, lo, hi; cohorts numbered from 1, the oldest, the oldest age group in the first period); fit, a named vector (deviance, df, loglik, iter, conv); and dims.

Details

The constraint is a choice, like any other that identifies the model: the age, period and cohort trends it reports are one of many that fit the same counts, and differ from another constraint's by a linear trend in each. The curvatures (deviations from the trends) are identified whatever the constraint.

References

Yang, Y., Fu, W. J. and Land, K. C. (2004). A methodological comparison of age-period-cohort models: the intrinsic estimator and conventional generalized linear models. Sociological Methodology, 34(1), 75-110. doi:10.1111/j.0081-1750.2004.00148.x

Examples

# arrests by five-year age group (rows) and five-year period (columns)
set.seed(11)
ag <- c(-1, 0.5, 0.2, -0.3, -0.6)
pe <- c(-0.2, 0, 0.1, 0.1)
co <- seq(-0.4, 0.4, length.out = 8)
ck <- outer(1:5, 1:4, function(i, j) j - i + 5)
eta <- outer(ag, pe, "+") + matrix(co[ck], 5)
pop <- matrix(1e5, 5, 4)
y <- matrix(rpois(20, pop * exp(-6 + eta)), 5,
            dimnames = list(c("15-19", "20-24", "25-29", "30-34", "35-39"),
                            c(2000, 2005, 2010, 2015)))
apcie(y, pop)
